Amazon break-even ACOS: how much can this listing still spend on ads?

Sellers search for “break-even ACOS” because Sponsored Products is managed as a percent of the sale price, not as a dollar on a spreadsheet. A 30% ACOS target is meaningless if referral, fulfillment, inbound, and the buy cost have already consumed the listing.

Break-even ACOS is the advertising spend that drives net profit to zero after every other cost on the selected fulfillment path. Target-margin ACOS is the lower spend that still leaves the net margin you typed. Both numbers change when you switch FBA to FBM, because storage and inbound are not the same as the label you buy yourself.

Generic ACOS pages often divide leftover margin by price and stop. They miss that FBA and FBM leave different leftover dollars on the same SKU, so they publish one campaign cap for two different cost stacks. Open the Amazon FBA vs FBM calculator, enter the rates from your current fee preview, and read break-even ACOS on each path next to the max buy cost.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advertising advice. It does not set a bid, and it does not claim a campaign will stay profitable after you change the spend.

What is break-even ACOS on Amazon?

Why is break-even ACOS different on FBA and FBM?

The leftover dollars change when storage and inbound replace the label you buy yourself. One campaign cap for both paths is two different cost stacks pretending to be one number.

Do Amazon returns wipe FBA profit?

Sellers search for “Amazon FBA return rate profit” because the number on a completed sale is not the number that hits the bank account. A slice of orders come back. Amazon typically refunds the buyer and the referral. The outbound pick fee, inbound, and storage do not come back. Cost of goods comes back only when the unit can be sold again.

On the $29.99 home listing — 15% referral, large-standard FBA at $4.15, $8.00 cost of goods, $1.20 inbound, one month of storage, and the professional plan spread over 80 units — a completed sale keeps $10.99. At a 15% return rate, $2.50 handling, and 20% of returns unsellable, expected profit is $7.75: $3.24 of drag. The return rate that wipes expected profit is about 50.9%. FBM on the same mix keeps $8.40 because there is no Amazon pick fee left spent on the returned unit.

Zero returns is always in the table so you can see the drag, not only the mixed number. Open the Amazon FBA calculator to change size, storage season, ads, or the seller plan. Aged leftover units are a different question — whether keeping them still beats a removal.

Do Amazon returns wipe FBA profit?

They can. The break-even return rate is the highest rate at which expected profit is still zero. It depends on the completed-sale leftover and how much cash one return still eats. Enter your fees and the return rate you actually see; this page is arithmetic, not a forecast of your category.

Does Amazon Subscribe & Save still pay after FBA fees?

Sellers search this after Amazon asks them to enroll a SKU and the 5% or 10% clip looks cheap next to a $29.99 list price. The discount is only half the hit. Referral is charged on the price the enrolled buyer actually pays. Fulfillment, inbound, and storage do not get cheaper because the unit is on a standing discount. Unlike a coupon, there is typically no per-redemption fee.

Open the Amazon FBA calculator, keep your own list price and fee preview, and enter the Subscribe & Save percent and the share of units you expect to enroll. The table below uses the page defaults: $29.99, 15% referral, large-standard FBA at $4.15, $8.00 cost of goods, $1.20 inbound, one month of storage, 80 units, 30% target margin, 40% enroll.

The example listing, then 5% Subscribe & Save

At list the unit keeps $10.99 (36.7%) and hits the 30% target. 5% S&S drops the buyer to $28.49. Referral falls with that price and profit is $9.72 (34.1%). That still hits the target. The same 5% coupon would leave $9.12 because of the $0.60 redemption fee.

Only some buyers enroll. If 40% of 80 units take 5% S&S (32 units), this month keeps $838.68 against $879.46 at list — $40.79 less. About 4.2 new S&S-only sales offset those converted buyers. A 15% promo on this listing leaves $7.17 (28.1%) and misses the target.

FBA vs FBM: which fulfillment path leaves more on the same listing?

Sellers search for “FBA vs FBM” because the referral fee is not the decision. Both fulfillment-by-Amazon and merchant-fulfilled listings usually pay the same category referral percentage. The gap is everything around it.

FBA adds a size-tier fulfillment fee, inbound to an Amazon warehouse, and monthly storage while the unit sits. Prime shipping is Amazon’s problem after that. FBM skips those Amazon fulfillment costs and replaces them with the label, packaging, and time you pay to ship the order yourself.

On a typical mid-price example — a $29.99 home-and-kitchen unit, 15% referral, a large-standard fulfillment default, $1.20 inbound, one month of storage, and a $4.75 merchant label — one path can keep several dollars more than the other. That difference is often larger than the referral-rate gap between categories.

Open the Amazon FBA vs FBM calculator, enter the numbers from your current fee preview, and compare both paths on one listing — including the maximum you can pay for the unit before it loses money. Neither is always cheaper. Yes. A unit that comes back usually refunds the referral fee but keeps the outbound pick fee, so the path that sees more returns loses more than a completed-sale comparison shows. Enter your own return rate before treating either path as the winner.

Is Amazon inbound placement cheaper than splitting the shipment?

Sellers search for “Amazon inbound placement fee” because the listing calculator’s inbound field hides the real trade. That number is usually freight plus placement blended into one unit cost. The decision Amazon actually offers on a create-shipment flow is three splits:

Send to one warehouse — cheapest freight, highest per-unit inbound placement fee. Partial split — more destinations, a mid placement fee. Amazon-optimized split — the destinations Amazon asks for, usually $0 placement, more freight and more labels.

On a 200-unit large-standard example — $85 to one warehouse, $140 for a partial split, $210 to follow Amazon’s split, and illustrative placement of $0.43 / $0.27 / $0 — one warehouse totals $171.00, the partial split $194.00, and the optimized split $210.00. Paying placement is $23.00 cheaper than the next option. The extra freight the optimized split can absorb before one warehouse wins is $86.00. Flip the freight quotes to $90 / $105 / $120 and a $0.55 minimal placement fee, and the optimized split wins by $80.00.

Should I use FBA or FBM for this product?

Start with the sale price. Should I stay under Amazon’s Low-Price FBA threshold — or raise the price?

Sellers keep a unit at $9.99 to stay in Amazon’s cheaper Low-Price FBA pick band, or they drop a $14 listing to $10 for the same reason. The referral fee is not the decision. Both prices usually pay the same category percentage. The gap is the pick fee versus the revenue you give up.

On a typical small-standard example — 15% referral, a $2.57 Low-Price pick fee against a $3.47 regular fee, $4 in the unit — staying at $9.99 keeps more. The regular path needs about $11.05 before the extra dollar of pick fee is paid for after referral: $9.99 + $0.90 ÷ 0.85. At $12, leaving the program keeps more. At $10.01 it does not.

The other direction is worse. Cutting a $29.99 home-and-kitchen listing to $10 to save ninety cents of fulfillment throws away most of the profit. The calculator shows both rows on the same cost of goods, inbound, and storage.

Should I price just over Amazon's Low-Price FBA threshold?

Usually no. The regular fulfillment fee jumps by more than one cent of extra revenue after the referral percentage. Enter your two pick fees in the calculator to see the raise that matches Low-Price profit.

Almost never. Losing several dollars of sale price to save less than a dollar of pick fee leaves less, after referral, on ordinary rates. Compare both prices on the same cost of goods before you cut the list price.

No. AWD is where a fresh US purchase order parks before it replenishes FBA. Inbound placement is which US fulfillment centers a shipment goes to. Remote Fulfillment is whether Canada or Mexico demand uses the US pile you already sent, for a per-unit surcharge, or whether you send a second pile across the border. This page holds US placement at the listing inbound line so the table stays a Canada-expansion question. It does not recommend Remote Fulfillment and it does not publish Amazon's live NARF schedule.

When does a dedicated Canada pile beat Remote Fulfillment?

When Canada inbound plus the slower Remote Fulfillment take costs more than sending working stock for local Prime. On these defaults a $2.40 Canada inbound flips the pile ahead by $1.57 per session ($6.69 vs $5.12). Matched take rates usually favor whichever inbound is cheaper. Should I use Seller Fulfilled Prime?

Sellers search this after Amazon invites the account to Seller Fulfilled Prime. FBA already has the Prime badge. SFP keeps that badge if you buy a 2-day label and pack on time. Merchant fulfilled is the cheaper Ground label without Prime. The main calculator’s FBA vs FBM table does not model that badge, so a completed-sale leftover can hide a take-rate gap.

On the default $29.99 large-standard unit, FBA keeps $4.03 more per session than SFP ($7.70 vs $3.67), $460.37 on 80 FBA units. Amazon’s $4.15 pick plus inbound is cheaper than an $8.95 2-day label and 6 minutes at $18. The 2-day label has to fall to about $2.75 before SFP matches. A $2.40 label flips SFP ahead by $0.23 per session, $26.20 a month. Merchant fulfilled keeps $11.64 on a completed sale but only $4.66 expected at 40% take — it needs about 66.1% to match FBA.

Path Take Ship / pick Completed Expected vs FBA

Expected leftover is take × completed sale on the same visitor pool (typed FBA units ÷ FBA take). Return mix is held at zero so this table stays a badge-and-label question. Should I leave FBA for Seller Fulfilled Prime?

The 2-day label has to fall to about $2.75 before SFP matches. Merchant fulfilled without Prime keeps $4.66 because the Ground label is cheaper, but 40% take is not enough; it needs about 66.1% to match FBA.

Is Seller Fulfilled Prime the same as FBM?

No. Seller Fulfilled Prime keeps the Prime badge, so take is usually close to FBA, but you buy a 2-day label and pack the order. Merchant fulfilled drops the Prime filter and usually converts fewer sessions. The page shows all three on the same visitor pool. It does not recommend a fulfillment method and it does not publish Amazon's live SFP SLA.

When does Seller Fulfilled Prime beat FBA?

When the 2-day label plus pack time is cheaper than Amazon's pick fee, inbound, and storage after the take-rate gap. On these defaults a $2.40 2-day label flips SFP ahead by $0.23 per session, $26.20 on 80 FBA units. A bulky pick fee can also flip the table. This calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

An FBA seller working more than one same-SKU decision -- FBA or FBM, a coupon, Subscribe & Save, a supplier MOQ, prep, inbound placement, Individual or Professional -- usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a row for the category referral rate, one for the size-tier fulfillment fee, a tab for the coupon math copied from the FBA-vs-FBM tab and edited by hand. This page is about what changes when those twenty comparisons stay wired to one listing instead of living in twenty cells someone has to remember to update together.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs. FBA versus FBM is a referral rate, a fulfillment fee, and a storage line against a shipping label. A coupon is the referral rate applied to a lower price, minus a redemption fee. A supplier MOQ is a lower unit cost against a longer warehouse stay. None of that needs anything a spreadsheet cannot do. Building it means pulling each rate from a different part of Seller Central or Amazon's help pages -- the category referral table, the size-tier fulfillment schedule, the placement-fee band, the current storage rate for the season -- typing each into the right cell, and adding a new tab the next time the listing needs a decision the sheet does not already have a row for.

This calculator keeps all twenty of those comparisons on one listing, already wired to the same sale price, cost of goods, and size tier, so changing the sale price updates the FBA-vs-FBM profit, the coupon lift needed, the MOQ break-even, and the rest at once instead of in whichever tabs got remembered. A shareable link carries the whole scenario in the URL, and named sourcing scenarios stay in your own browser so you can switch between two suppliers or two price points without retyping eighty fields.

The gap is not that the arithmetic differs. On this calculator's own shipped listing -- a $29.99 large-standard item, $8 cost of goods, 80 units a month, and the illustrative defaults -- FBA nets $10.99 and FBM nets $11.64: a $0.65 gap that a spreadsheet reproduces correctly only if someone remembered to point its FBM tab at the same sale price and cost-of-goods cells as its FBA tab, and re-checks that link every time either number changes.

A spreadsheet is not a worse tool so much as a shortcut whose upkeep cost is easy to underweight until a tab goes stale after a rate changes. This calculator does not remove that flexibility -- your own sheet can still model anything this one's fixed fields cannot -- it just keeps the twenty decisions most FBA sellers actually repeat wired to one listing instead of twenty cells.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Every comparison this calculator runs -- FBA versus FBM, a coupon against list price, Subscribe & Save against list, a supplier MOQ against your usual order, Amazon prep against you-prep, inbound placement against split freight, Individual against Professional, Low-Price FBA against a real raise, aged inventory against a removal, AWD against send-all-to-FBA, Remote Fulfillment against skipping Canada, and Seller Fulfilled Prime against FBA -- is ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Getting there means pulling your category's referral rate, your size tier's fulfillment fee, the season's storage rate, and the placement, prep, and account-fee schedules from separate parts of Seller Central or Amazon's help pages, then typing each into the right cell.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep all twenty of those comparisons wired to the same listing so changing one number -- the sale price, the cost of goods, the return rate -- updates every comparison built on it at once. A sheet built for the FBA-vs-FBM decision rarely already has a tab for a coupon, a MOQ, or a Remote Fulfillment surcharge on the same SKU, so each new decision usually means a new tab copied from an old one, with its own chance of a stale formula or a rate that was never updated after the last one changed. This calculator also produces a shareable link that carries the whole listing after the # in the URL, and named scenarios kept in your own browser, neither of which a spreadsheet file does without emailing it around.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a shape this calculator's inputs cannot represent -- a bundle of several ASINs in one shipment, a private-label deal with a rebate structure, or a fee schedule from a program this tool does not model. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one listing moving through the fulfillment, pricing, and inbound decisions most FBA sellers actually face.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, named sourcing scenarios stay in your own browser's storage, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day -- never your prices, costs, or ASIN.
